title: Session 2 — Income Statement: Accrual vs Cash Accounting
summary: BBM140 Financial Reporting and Analysis — the structure of the Income Statement, the accrual, matching and prudence principles, why profit and cash differ, accruals and deferrals, revenue recognition (IFRS 15 / IFRS 9), and impairment of receivables (doubtful and bad debt).

blocks.title: 🎯 Learning objectives
items: Learn the structure and components of the Income Statement.
Learn the accounting principles of revenue recognition, matching and prudence.
Understand the differences between cash numbers and accrual accounting numbers.
Learn the concepts of provision/impairment for doubtful debts and bad debt expense.

blocks.title: 1. What the Income Statement is
blocks.content:
The **Income Statement (I/S)** — the profit & loss account — is a **summary of the financial performance of the business over one reporting period**. It is a **statement of flows**: it reports how **equity (shareholders' wealth) increased or decreased** as a result of business activities.

$$\text{Profit / Loss} = \text{Revenues} - \text{Expenses}$$

The bottom-line measure of value added to (or lost from) equity is **net profit / loss**. Whereas the Balance Sheet is a *snapshot* at a point in time, the Income Statement links two balance sheets by explaining the change in equity from trading.

blocks.title: 2. Components of profit
blocks.content:
**Revenues**
- **Operating revenue** — sales of products or services (units sold × selling price).
- **Non-operating income** — interest income from financial investments; profit from selling non-current assets.

**Expenses**
- **Cost of goods sold (COGS)** — units sold × production/purchase cost.
- **Operating expenses** — administration, marketing, distribution, R&D, depreciation.
- **Non-operating expenses** — finance costs (interest expense); loss from selling non-current assets.

blocks.title: 3. When are revenues and expenses recognised? — the accrual principle
blocks.content:
The **accrual principle**: **revenue is recognised when it is *earned* and expenses when they are *incurred*, rather than when money is received or paid.** Expenses are **matched** to the revenue they helped to generate.

**Cool Phones plc example.** The firm has cash £85,000, inventory £35,000, share capital £100,000, accounts payable £20,000. It **sells 20% of inventory (cost £7,000) to a client *on credit* for £12,000**:

- **Trade receivables +£12,000** (client owes us — recognised even though no cash yet).
- **Inventory −£7,000** (goods delivered leave the business).
- The difference, **£5,000 = £12,000 − £7,000, is the profit** — wealth generated by trading, which belongs to shareholders, so **equity +£5,000**.

Only the **cost of the inventory *sold*** (£7,000) is matched against sales revenue — **not** the whole £35,000 of inventory. The unsold inventory (£35,000 − £7,000 = **£28,000**) stays on the balance sheet and will be charged against **future** sales revenue when it is sold.

blocks.title: 4. Key Income Statement terms
blocks.content:
| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Gross profit** | Profit from buying/producing and selling = **Sales revenue − Cost of goods sold** |
| **Operating expenses** | Costs of generating revenue: salaries, advertising, distribution, depreciation, overheads |
| **Operating profit (EBIT)** | What remains after removing operating expenses from gross profit |
| **Net profit** | Operating profit − non-operating expenses + non-operating income |

The I/S 'waterfalls' down: **Sales → Gross profit → Operating profit (EBIT) → Net profit**.

blocks.title: 5. Principles of accrual accounting
blocks.content:
**Single-period vs multi-period.** Accounting in a *single-period* world is easy — think of a 15th-century shipping voyage: the ship is sold at the end, so **income is simply cash in − cash out**. But a real firm is a **going concern** with no predetermined end, cash flows in and out at many points, and external investors need performance measured **at particular points in time**. Hence **accrual accounting**, which aims to measure performance in a period *independently of when cash changes hands*.

**Going concern:** we assume the business will continue for the foreseeable future. If instead we expected it to close, we might use market values, record extra liabilities (e.g. redundancy) and write assets up/down to realisable value.

**Revenue recognition principle** — recognise revenue when:
1. the earnings process is **substantially complete** (control/risks & rewards transferred to the buyer), and
2. **cash collection is reasonably assured**.

> A sale on credit is recognised **when goods are transferred to the client, not when cash is received.**

**Matching principle for expenses** — match efforts to the benefits generated:
- **Capitalise** expenditure that will generate **future** benefits; **expense** it when the benefits are realised.
- Recognise **liabilities** when current-period efforts require **future** cash payment.

blocks.title: 6. Matching — the mechanics
blocks.content:
Revenues earned are **matched** with the expenses incurred in earning them. An expense can be **deferred** until the related revenue is recognised **only if** it meets the definition of an **asset**.

**Example — sale on credit:**
- Sales revenue is recognised in the I/S when goods are **transferred** to the client (not only when cash is received).
- The **cost of sale** is recognised at the *same time*, to match the expense with the revenue.

Inventory bought but **unsold** is **not** expensed now — its cost stays in **assets** on the balance sheet until it is sold, when it becomes cost of sale matched against future revenue.

blocks.title: 7. Prudence (conservatism)
blocks.content:
The **prudence principle**: a degree of **caution** should be applied in exercising judgment and making estimates.

- **Gains** are treated as realised **only when realised** — as cash, or as other assets whose ultimate cash realisation is reasonably certain.
- There is **no such requirement for losses** → **losses are recognised faster than gains.**

**Examples:**
- Doubts about a client's ability to pay → **reduce profit immediately** "as if" the client will not pay.
- Stock bought for £1,000 is now worth £1,500 → **do not** recognise the £500 gain until the stock is actually sold.

*Why?* Shareholders are keener to learn **sooner** about potential future **losses** than about potential future gains.

blocks.title: 8. Cash vs accounting profit — Teddington Bookstore
blocks.content:
Accounting profit tracks **economic** profit (when value is generated or consumed), **not** cash. Timing of receipts/payments is irrelevant — what matters is when revenue and expenses are **recognised**. **In one reporting period, profit and cash are NOT the same.**

**Teddington Bookstore** over three weeks:
- **Week 1:** buy books for **£10,000 cash**.
- **Week 2:** sell all books **on credit for £15,000**.
- **Week 3:** receive **£15,000** from customers.

| | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 3 | End of business |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | | 15,000 | | 15,000 |
| Expense | | 10,000 | | 10,000 |
| **Profit (I/S, accrual)** | – | **5,000** | – | **5,000** |
| Cash inflow | | | 15,000 | 15,000 |
| Cash outflow | 10,000 | | | 10,000 |
| **Net cash** | **(10,000)** | – | **15,000** | **5,000** |

- **Week 1:** merchandise is *stocked* as an asset — no I/S impact — but cash falls £10,000.
- **Week 2:** revenue and matching cost of sale are recognised (profit £5,000) even though **no cash moves**.
- **Week 3:** £15,000 cash arrives but **profit is unaffected**.

**Over the whole life of the business, total profit = total cash generated (£5,000)** — but in individual periods they diverge, because cash flows and the revenues/expenses they relate to fall in different periods.

blocks.title: 9. Accruals and deferrals — four transactions
blocks.content:
Because revenue/expense may be recognised in a **different period** than the related cash flow, four types of item appear on the balance sheet:

| | **Not yet paid/received in cash** | **Paid/received in cash but not yet recognised** |
|---|---|---|
| **Expenses** | **Accrued expense** — consumed but not paid (e.g. accrued salaries) → *liability* | **Deferred (prepaid) expense** — paid but not consumed (e.g. prepaid insurance) → *asset* |
| **Revenues** | **Accrued revenue** — earned but not received (e.g. accrued interest income) → *asset* | **Deferred (unearned) revenue** — received but not earned (e.g. unearned rent) → *liability* |

- **Accruals** arise when goods/services are **received/earned in advance of the cash**.
- **Deferrals (prepayments)** arise when the **cash moves in advance** of the goods/services.

blocks.title: 10. Accrued expenses — Acacia Ltd
blocks.content:
When the **expense for the period exceeds the cash paid**, record a **liability** for the incurred-but-unpaid amount. If a bill/invoice has been received → classify it as a **trade payable / accounts payable**; if **no** invoice yet → classify it as an **accrued expense**.

**Acacia Ltd** (year-end 31 Dec 2025):

**(a) Electricity — invoice received.** £500 bill for Nov/Dec 2025, to be paid Jan 2026.

| | Cash | Accounts payable | Profit (I/S) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025 — electricity expense | | +500 | (500) |
| 2026 — payment of bill | (500) | (500) | |

**(b) Telephone — no invoice yet, estimated £1,000.**

| | Cash | Accrued expense | Accounts payable | Profit (I/S) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025 — telephone expense | | +1,000 | | (1,000) |
| 2026 — receipt of bill | | (1,000) | +1,000 | |
| 2026 — payment of bill | (1,000) | | (1,000) | |

**Effect of omitting the 2025 entry:** liabilities **understated by £1,000** and earnings **overstated by £1,000**.

*If the actual bill is £1,100:* the extra £100 not accrued becomes a 2026 expense (profit (100) in 2026), because only £1,000 had been estimated.

blocks.title: 11. Prepaid (deferred) expenses — insurance
blocks.content:
When the **amount paid exceeds the expense for the period**, a **prepayment** arises (cash paid before the expense is incurred). The prepaid amount is a **current asset**; next period it ceases to be an asset and becomes an expense.

**Example:** on **1 Sep 2026** a company pays a **£1,200** insurance premium for the year to 30 Aug 2027; year-end is **31 Dec**.

- Usage in 2026 = 1,200 ÷ 12 × **4 months** = **£400** expense.
- **Prepayment carried to 2027** = 1,200 − 400 = **£800** (asset).
- Usage in 2027 = 1,200 ÷ 12 × **8 months** = **£800** expense (cancels the prepayment).

| | Prepayments (asset) | Cash | Profit (I/S) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 — payment of insurance | | (1,200) | (1,200) |
| 2026 — defer to 2027 | +800 | | +800 |
| 2027 — insurance expense | (800) | | (800) |

**Effect of omitting the deferral:** assets **understated by £800** and retained earnings (equity) **understated by £800**.

blocks.title: 12. Deferred (unearned) revenue — Country Residence plc
blocks.content:
When the business **receives cash in advance** of providing goods/services, record the **cash** but **not** the revenue — revenue must be recognised when *earned*. Set up a **liability: unearned/deferred revenue**.

**Country Residence plc** (letting agency, year-end 31 Dec). At end-Dec 2025 it receives **£2,000** of rent for **Jan & Feb 2026**:

| | Cash | Deferred revenue (liability) | Profit (I/S) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025 — receipt of 2026 rents | +2,000 | +2,000 | |
| 2026 — rents earned | | (2,000) | +2,000 |

**Effect of omitting the entry:** liabilities **overstated by £2,000** and retained earnings (equity) **understated by £2,000** — wait, note the lecture's phrasing: omitting the *earning* entry in 2026 would leave liabilities overstated and equity understated by £2,000.

blocks.title: 13. Accrued revenue — Gameover plc (bond interest)
blocks.content:
When revenue is **earned but cash will only be received in a future period**, recognise the revenue now and set up an **asset: accrued revenue (income)**.

Under **IFRS 9**, interest is recognised **proportionately to the length of the period** the asset was made available, at the agreed rate.

**Gameover plc:** on 1 Oct 2026 it invests **£100,000** in government bonds paying **5% annually every 30 Sep**; year-end 31 Dec.

- Interest earned in **2026** (Oct–Dec, 3 months) = 100,000 × 5% ÷ 12 × 3 = **£1,250**.
- Interest earned in **2027** (9 months to 30 Sep + …) = 100,000 × 5% ÷ 12 × 9 = **£3,750**.

| | Cash | Accrued revenue (asset) | Profit (I/S) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 — interest receivable | | +1,250 | +1,250 |
| 2027 — receipt of 2026 interest | +1,250 | (1,250) | |
| 2027 — interest earned & received | +3,750 | | +3,750 |

blocks.title: 14. Revenue recognition rules (IFRS 15)
15. Bad and doubtful debt — the problem
16. Doubtful debt — Zett plc (recognition in X1)
blocks.content:
**Zett plc:** in **X1** it sells goods for **£15,000** on 3-month credit. During X1 the client pays only **£14,000** and, despite chasing, does not pay the remaining **£1,000**. In **X2** the client reports financial difficulties and the debt is declared 'difficult to collect'.

**When should the loss be recognised?** Recognising it *only* in X2 (doing nothing in X1) is **not prudent**. Leaving it out of X1 would **overstate assets** (receivables) by £1,000 **and overstate profit** by £1,000.

**Both principles point to X1:**
- **Prudence** → recognise the expense in X1, assuming the worst case (not collecting).
- **Accrual/matching** → recognise the expense in X1 to match the revenue from the same sale (also X1).

**Accounting entries in X1:**

| | Cash | Impairment (contra asset) | Accounts receivable | Profit (I/S) | Retained profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sale | | | +15,000 | +15,000 | |
| Receipt from sales | +14,000 | | (14,000) | | |
| Impairment | | (1,000) | | (1,000) | |
| Transfer to retained profit | | | | (14,000) | +14,000 |
| **Closing balance** | **14,000** | **(1,000)** | **1,000** | **0** | **14,000** |

In the **B/S**, impairment is shown as a deduction from receivables (Receivables 1,000 *less* Impairment (1,000) = 0 net). In the **I/S**, the **impairment loss is a separate operating expense** — it is **not** netted against sales revenue.

blocks.title: 17. Reversal of impairment — Zett plc in X2
blocks.content:
In **X2** the client's troubles are resolved: they agree to pay **60%** of the £1,000 debt; the remaining **40%** becomes a genuine **bad debt**. The credit is resolved, so the impairment allowance is no longer needed and is **reversed**.

| | Cash | Impairment | Accounts receivable | Profit (I/S) | Retained profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opening balance | 14,000 | (1,000) | 1,000 | | 14,000 |
| Cash received (600) & bad debt (400) | +600 | | (1,000) | (400) | |
| Reversal of impairment | | +1,000 | | +1,000 | |
| Transfer to retained profit | | | | (600) | +600 |
| **Closing balance** | **14,600** | **0** | **0** | **0** | **14,600** |

So £600 is collected, £400 is charged as **bad debt expense**, and the £1,000 allowance is **cancelled** against the I/S. *Note:* as an alternative to an allowance account, the receivable can be reduced directly; impairment is assessed **individually**, but receivables that are individually insignificant can be **grouped** by similar credit risk and tested collectively.

items.definition: A statement of flows summarising performance over a period; explains how equity changed from trading. Profit = Revenues − Expenses.
Recognise revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash is received or paid.
Match expenses to the revenue they help generate; defer an expense only if it meets the definition of an asset.
Exercise caution: recognise losses faster than gains; recognise gains only when realised.
Assume the business will continue for the foreseeable future (so historical cost, not liquidation values, applies).

items.term: Gross vs operating vs net profit
items.definition: Gross = sales − COGS; Operating (EBIT) = gross − operating expenses; Net = operating − non-operating expenses + non-operating income.
Expense incurred but not yet paid — a liability (e.g. accrued salaries, estimated telephone bill).
Cash paid before the expense is incurred — a current asset (e.g. prepaid insurance).
Revenue earned but cash not yet received — an asset (e.g. accrued interest income).
Cash received before revenue is earned — a liability (e.g. rent received in advance).
Revenue is recognised when control/risks & rewards transfer, amounts and costs are measurable, and benefits are probable (goods and services).
A receivable reasonably certain not to be collected; written off — reduces receivables and creates an expense.
An allowance (contra asset) for receivables in doubt; an I/S expense recognised on objective evidence of a loss event.
An account that reduces a related asset (e.g. allowance for doubtful debt reducing gross receivables).

blocks.title: 🧪 Try it yourself — cash vs profit, and prepaid/accrued split
blocks.prompt: Reproduce the Teddington Bookstore cash-vs-profit result, then split the insurance premium and the bond interest across periods. Change the timings and see how period profit and period cash diverge while the totals still tie out.
blocks.starter:
# --- Teddington Bookstore: profit vs cash over 3 weeks ---
revenue   = [0, 15_000, 0]
expense   = [0, 10_000, 0]
cash_in   = [0, 0, 15_000]
cash_out  = [10_000, 0, 0]

for w in range(3):
    profit = revenue[w] - expense[w]
    netcash = cash_in[w] - cash_out[w]
    print(f"Week {w+1}: profit={profit:>7,}  net cash={netcash:>8,}")
print(f"TOTAL : profit={sum(revenue)-sum(expense):>7,}  net cash={sum(cash_in)-sum(cash_out):>8,}")

# --- Prepaid insurance: 1,200 paid 1 Sep for 12 months, year-end 31 Dec ---
premium, months_used_2026 = 1_200, 4
exp_2026 = premium/12 * months_used_2026
prepaid  = premium - exp_2026
print(f"\nInsurance 2026 expense = {exp_2026:.0f}, prepayment carried to 2027 = {prepaid:.0f}")

# --- Accrued interest: 100,000 @ 5%, invested 1 Oct, year-end 31 Dec ---
accrued_2026 = 100_000 * 0.05 / 12 * 3
print(f"Accrued interest income 2026 = {accrued_2026:.0f}")

cards.back: Recognise revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, not when cash is received or paid; match expenses to the revenue they generate.

cards.front: When is a credit sale's revenue recognised?
cards.back: When goods/control are transferred to the client — not when cash is received.
Losses are recognised faster than gains; gains only when realised. Shareholders want early warning of losses.

cards.front: Over a business's whole life, how do total profit and total cash compare?
cards.back: They are equal. They differ only period-by-period because of timing.
Prepaid = cash paid before expense incurred (asset). Accrued = expense incurred before cash paid (liability).
Deferred = cash received before earned (liability). Accrued = earned before cash received (asset).

cards.front: Where does an impairment loss on receivables appear?
cards.back: A separate operating expense in the I/S; in the B/S a contra asset reduces gross receivables. It is NOT netted against sales.

cards.front: Why recognise doubtful debt in the sale year, not later?
cards.back: Prudence (assume worst case) AND matching (match the loss to the revenue from the same sale).

questions.q: A firm sells goods on credit in December but is paid in February. Under accrual accounting, when is the revenue recognised?
options: In February, when cash is received
In December, when the goods are transferred
Only when the customer confirms payment
questions.explanation: Revenue is recognised when earned (goods/control transferred) in December, regardless of when cash arrives.

questions.q: Teddington buys books for £10,000 cash (Wk1), sells all on credit for £15,000 (Wk2), collects £15,000 (Wk3). What is Week 2's profit and net cash?
questions.explanation: Week 2 recognises revenue 15,000 and cost of sale 10,000 → profit 5,000, but no cash moves that week → net cash 0.

questions.q: A £1,200 insurance premium is paid on 1 Sep for 12 months; the year ends 31 Dec. What is this year's expense and the prepayment carried forward?
questions.explanation: 4 months used this year: 1,200/12×4 = £400 expense; the remaining £800 is a prepaid (deferred) expense, a current asset.

questions.q: Rent for next January and February (£2,000) is received in December. How is it recorded in December?
options: As revenue in the Income Statement
questions.explanation: Cash received before it is earned is deferred/unearned revenue — a liability — recognised as revenue only when earned next year.

questions.q: Under prudence and matching, when should Zett recognise the loss on a doubtful receivable from an X1 sale?
options: In X2, once the client reports difficulty
In X1, matching the loss to the sale's revenue and assuming the worst case
Never, unless the client formally defaults
questions.explanation: Recognise the allowance in X1: prudence assumes the worst case, and matching ties the loss to the X1 sale revenue. Waiting overstates X1 assets and profit.

questions.q: How is an allowance for doubtful debt presented?
options: Deducted from sales revenue in the I/S
As a contra asset reducing receivables (B/S) and a separate expense (I/S)
As a liability on the balance sheet
As a reduction of share capital
questions.explanation: It is a contra (negative) asset that reduces gross receivables in the B/S, with a separate impairment expense in the I/S — not netted against sales.

blocks.title: 📝 Recap
blocks.content: The Income Statement is a statement of flows (Profit = Revenues − Expenses) explaining how trading changed equity over a period. Under the accrual principle, revenue is recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, matched to that revenue, while prudence recognises losses faster than gains. Because recognition and cash timing differ, profit ≠ cash within a period (Teddington: totals tie out over the whole life), giving rise to four items: accrued and prepaid expenses, and accrued and deferred revenues. Revenue recognition follows IFRS 15 (transfer of control, measurability) and interest follows IFRS 9 (time-proportion). Doubtful debts are impaired in the year of sale via a contra-asset allowance and a separate I/S expense (prudence + matching), reversing when the doubt is resolved and crystallising any bad debt.
